description.value: An fMRI study examined whether a bitter wormwood-tea aftertaste changes neural responses to visual high- and low-caloric food cues and whether appetite reduction correlates with brain activation.

spans.text: The current fMRI study aimed at demonstrating that bitter aftertaste is able to change neuronal and affective responses to pleasant visual food cues.

value: It was hypothesized that the bitter taste would reduce the appetite with regard to the displayed food items.
we expected increased activation in brain regions involved in appetite regulation such as the insula, striatum, OFC, and DLPFC
Finally, it was investigated if the degree of appetite reduction correlates with brain activation in these brain regions of interest.

description.value: Slice timing, motion correction with realignment and unwarping, field-map correction, coregistration, normalization to MNI space, and 8 mm Gaussian smoothing.

spans.text: In the first step, acquisition timing was accounted during the slice timing step, using the middle slice as reference scan. In the second step, motion correction was done using realignment and unwarping with an additional field map that should correct additionally for possible field inhomogeneity. Subsequently, individuals T1-weighted images were segmented into grey matter (GM), white matter (WM) and cerebrospinal fluid and a skull-stripped image was created. Slice-timed, realigned and unwarped images were matched to the skull-stripped image using the normalized mutual function. Afterwards obtained deformations fields were used to bring functional images to MNI-space. Finally, images were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 8 mm.
All analyses were conducted using SPM12 (version: 6906; Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, London).
